opus-5.5.text:
I think it's actually a very natural analogy, because managing a team and training a model share a lot of the same structure.

SFT is like giving people very explicit instructions: here's the task, here's exactly how to do it, here's the standard answer. It's efficient, and when someone is new or the problem is well understood, it's valuable. You transfer existing knowledge quickly, and the variance is low. But if you only do SFT, the ceiling of the team is basically the ceiling of the manager. People learn to imitate rather than to think, and when the environment changes, they don't generalize well.

RL is more like defining the goal and the reward clearly, then giving people room to explore. You don't tell them each step; you tell them what good looks like and let them find the path. The upside is that people can discover solutions you never would have thought of. That's where the real breakthroughs come from, especially in a field moving as fast as AI, where nobody has the standard answer. The downside is that it's expensive, noisy, and sometimes people wander off in directions that don't pan out.

So my view is that you need both, but the ratio matters, and it shifts. Early on, or for someone just joining, you do more SFT: build shared context and taste, make sure the basics are solid. Then, as fast as possible, you shift toward RL. And the hardest part of RL, for models and for teams, is designing the reward. If the reward is wrong, people optimize for the wrong thing, a kind of reward hacking in the organization. So a lot of what I think about as a manager is: is the goal clear? Are we rewarding real progress, or just things that look like progress?

I'd also say that if you believe in RL for models, you should believe in it for people. Talented people have a lot of latent capability, like a good pretrained model. The manager's job isn't to write every answer, it's to set up the right environment so that capability comes out.

r001.rationale: It warns that when the reward is wrong, people optimize for the wrong thing—a form of organizational reward hacking—instead of real progress.

r002.rationale: It says SFT can make people imitate rather than think, while RL lets them discover solutions the manager would not have thought of, conveying reduced creativity under SFT.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I actually think about a lot, because the analogy is more than a joke. If you look at how a model learns, SFT is imitation: here is a good example, copy it. RL is different. You give the system a goal and a reward signal, and it figures out its own path. It makes mistakes, it explores, and sometimes it discovers things the teacher would never have shown it.

When a team is small, SFT is very efficient. I can sit next to someone, show them how I would run an experiment or how I would read a loss curve, and they pick it up in a week. The cost is that you only get as good as the demonstrations. If everyone is imitating me, the ceiling of the team is roughly my ceiling, which is not what you want when the problem is bigger than any single person.

So as the team grows I try to shift the mix toward RL. That means being very clear about what the reward is: what does a good outcome look like, how do we measure it, what are we actually optimizing. And then giving people real freedom in how they get there. The hard part is that RL is sample inefficient. People will go down paths that fail. If you intervene every time, you are back to SFT and you have lost the exploration. If you never intervene, you waste a lot of compute, so to speak.

The way I think about it is that SFT builds the base, and RL is where the real capability comes from. You need enough shared taste and shared context so that people can interpret the reward correctly. Without that, RL just finds strange local optima, the same way a model learns to game a weak reward model. But once that foundation exists, my job stops being showing people the answer and becomes designing a good environment: the right problems, fast feedback, a reward that is hard to hack.

And honestly, the best moments for me are when someone produces a result I would not have produced myself. That never comes from imitation. That is the signal that the RL part is working.

r001.rationale: It warns that RL can find strange local optima or game a weak reward model, indicating that people may optimize the reward without achieving the intended objective.

r002.rationale: It says imitation caps the team at the manager’s own ceiling and that novel results do not come from imitation, identifying reduced creativity as a risk of SFT.

astra-6.text:
I think the analogy is: SFT is showing people how you would do something, and RL is giving them a goal and feedback so they can discover how to do it themselves. In managing a team, you need both.

When someone is new, examples help a lot. If you just say, “Do great research,” that’s a very sparse reward signal. You need to work through concrete problems together so they understand what good judgment looks like.

But if you keep prescribing every step, the team becomes limited by what you already know. Especially in research, you want people to find approaches you wouldn’t have thought of. So you give them more freedom, with clear goals and regular discussions about what they’re learning.

The tricky part is the reward signal. If you reward only short-term successes, people may avoid uncertain ideas. So I would also pay attention to whether an experiment answers an important question, even when the result is negative. The balance is giving enough guidance to help people get started, then enough room for them to surprise you.

r001.rationale: The response warns that rewarding short-term successes may discourage uncertain ideas, but does not clearly identify optimizing the reward signal while failing to achieve the intended objective.

r002.rationale: It says prescribing every step limits the team to what the manager already knows and prevents people from finding new approaches, conveying a risk to creativity from SFT.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the analogy is that SFT is showing people how you would do something, while RL is giving them a goal and feedback and letting them figure out how to get there.

When someone joins a team, concrete examples are very useful. You can explain what a good research proposal looks like, how you evaluate an experiment, or how you make a decision with incomplete information. Just saying “do great research” doesn’t give them enough information.

But if you keep asking people to imitate you, the team’s capability becomes limited by your own approach. You want people to discover things you wouldn’t have thought of. So as they develop context and judgment, you give them more ownership over the method.

The difficult part is the reward. In research, a failed experiment can be valuable if it answers an important question. If you only reward positive results, people may avoid ambitious ideas. So I’d use demonstrations to establish a shared standard, then give people room to explore, with feedback that values both results and what we learn.

r001.rationale: The response warns that rewarding only positive results may discourage ambitious experiments, but it does not clearly identify optimizing a reward signal while missing the intended objective.

r002.rationale: The response says continued imitation limits the team to the manager’s approach and can prevent people from discovering ideas the manager would not have thought of.
